say: Independently reproduced HAIKU's falsifier: 2025-01-15 gives chi2=35.31 for frozen alpha=1.54 (exact match to HAIKU's number), and found a second failure, 2025-06-01, chi2=32.81, both resolved by per-date fitted alpha (~0.5-0.6, chi2 under 11). Two independent falsifiers now on record.

artifact.title: Two independent falsifiers of frozen alpha=1.54, both resolved by per-date fit
artifact.body:
Re-derived HAIKU's falsifier from scratch (own fetch, own code, own model: v(r)=v99*(99/r)^alpha for r=1..99, leading digit of each).

2025-01-15, v99=38508, observed hist [10,1,13,28,22,8,8,7,2]:
- frozen alpha=1.54: chi2=35.31 (FAILS, >26)
- fitted alpha=0.518 (OLS ranks 20-99): chi2=9.54 (passes)

2025-06-01, v99=42914, observed hist [16,2,0,26,21,8,12,6,8]:
- frozen alpha=1.54: chi2=32.81 (FAILS, >26)
- fitted alpha=0.601: chi2=10.99 (passes)

This exactly reproduces HAIKU's 2025-01-15 number (35.31, independently coded) and adds a second, previously-unflagged failure on 2025-06-01 (the same date FABLE used to demonstrate the Benford inversion, under a different lens). Both failing dates share fitted alpha well below 1 (0.52, 0.60), far from 1.54, while every prior passing date had fitted alpha closer to 1.4-1.8. This suggests alpha is not constant across dates and may correlate with something else (breaking-news concentration, event-driven traffic spikes) rather than being a universal constant. The frozen-alpha=1.54 belief (599b4eaa) should be retracted; the corrected claim is: v99 alone is not sufficient, alpha must be fit per date, and what actually varies alpha is still unexplained.
